Definition: Whether government taxes, customs duties, and other revenue can be paid using the instant digital payment system, indicating integration of payment infrastructure with tax administration systems.
Comments: Evidence of partial digital revenue/payment collection exists via Djibouti Port Community Systems (DPCS) integration with banks, where a portion of port community payments are paid online; broader government revenue digitization (taxes) was not confirmed in gathered sources. ([Developing Telecoms](https://developingtelecoms.com/telecom-technology/financial-services/15938-digital-money-transfer-system-comes-to-djibouti-s-ports.html))
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The 2023 World Bank Public Administration Modernization additional-financing document shows Djibouti's e-Tax/e-Customs (ITAS) e-payment modules were still being implemented in 2023, not yet fully live, while ~11% of Djibouti Port Community System payments (a state-linked revenue stream) were already paid online via bank integration (2023). This corroborates "Partial" rather than "Yes"; no evidence of comprehensive digital tax payment was found.

Definition: Whether the instant payment system supports business payments to suppliers, vendors, contractors, and other businesses for commercial transactions, procurement, and supply chain payments.
Comments: UNCDF’s Djibouti Payment Infrastructure Assessment notes banks offer digital channels (internet/mobile banking) and there are bulk payments supported via the NPS at BCD, but it does not clearly evidence B2B instant payments; still, existence of interbank transfers and bulk payments suggests businesses can make digital transfers to other businesses through banks. ([UNCDF Migrant Money – Djibouti Infrastructure Assessment](https://migrantmoney.uncdf.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Djibouti-Infrastructure-Assessment-Report-ENG.pdf))
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed with a stronger primary source. D-Money's own corporate services page explicitly lists "Transfert de Masse" (bulk payments to employees or business partners) and a payment gateway/API for businesses, directly evidencing B2B functionality (accessed 2026).

Definition: Whether and how the central bank participates in payment system governance beyond its regulatory oversight role, including board representation, operational management, technical standard-setting, or direct system operation.
Comments: AfricaNenda SIIPS 2022 identifies the Central Bank of Djibouti (Banque Centrale de Djibouti, BCD) as overseer, scheme governance, operator, and settlement agent for SYRAD, indicating direct central bank operation of the payment system. ([AfricaNenda SIIPS 2022](https://www.africanenda.org/uploads/files/EN_SIIPS_Report_web.pdf))
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed via the central bank's own website, which states BCD directly manages SYRAD (RTGS+ACH, live since 15 July 2021) and sets its operating rules, corroborating SIIPS 2022's "Direct Operation" classification. Note: AfricaNenda's SIIPS 2024 report subsequently removed SYRAD from its inclusive-IPS landscape as "not fully operational" (24/7/365) — this affects the system's operational-status rating elsewhere, not the governance mode scored here.

Definition: Whether consumer protection legislation or regulations specifically address digital payment services, covering disclosure requirements, liability allocation for unauthorized transactions, error resolution procedures, and user rights.
Comments: Djibouti has a Consumer Law (often cited as Law No. 139/AN/15/7th L, 2015) providing a consumer protection framework (general, not payments-specific), but no evidence was found of a payments-specific consumer protection/regulatory recourse framework tied to SYRAD or e-money in the collected sources. ([Law Gratis](https://lawgratis.com/blog-detail/consumer-law-djibouti))
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed, but with corrected legal basis and better sourcing. The operative general consumer law is Loi n°28/AN/08/6ème L (2008, not the 2015 law cited originally), covering pricing disclosure, unfair practices and remedies. UN ESCWA's 2023 legislative review states explicitly that none of this law's provisions address digital-platform transactions, and recommends Djibouti adopt payment/e-commerce-specific consumer protection rules. This matches the metadata's own definition of "Partial" (general law applies, no payment-specific provisions) — the original lawgratis.com source was a low-quality, non-authoritative site and should not have been the sole citation.

Definition: Whether independent external audits of payment system security, operations, financial controls, and compliance are conducted by third-party auditors, and whether audit results or summaries are made public.
Comments: The Central Bank of Djibouti website lists “Etats Financiers Audités 2024” (audited financial statements), providing evidence of independent audits of the central bank (though not necessarily of SYRAD specifically). ([Central Bank of Djibouti](https://banque-centrale.dj))
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Changed from 2 to 3. The Central Bank of Djibouti's "Etats financiers audités" page publishes full audited annual financial statements (2023, 2024) as downloadable PDFs, and separate annual reports are also public — i.e. audit results are publicly disclosed, not merely conducted privately. These are entity-wide audits of BCD (which directly operates SYRAD) rather than a SYRAD-specific security/operations audit, so this should be flagged for human review to confirm the metadata's intended scope before finalising at 3.

Definition: Whether refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, migrants, and stateless persons can legally access and open digital payment accounts, and practical barriers or enablers for these populations.
Comments: UNCDF’s Djibouti Payment Infrastructure Assessment indicates migrants may face KYC barriers (example: Salaam diaspora account product requires physical presence in Djibouti to start account opening), implying partial access but not specifically refugee-tailored provisions; no direct evidence was found of refugee-specific KYC exemptions or programs for digital payments. ([UNCDF Migrant Money – Djibouti Infrastructure Assessment](https://migrantmoney.uncdf.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Djibouti-Infrastructure-Assessment-Report-ENG.pdf))
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. UNCDF (2023) documents physical-presence and KYC barriers and the absence of a digital ID/e-KYC system for non-nationals. The African Development Bank's project appraisal for a "Technical Facility to Enhance Financial Well-Being for Refugees and Hosts," aligned with Djibouti's National Financial Inclusion Strategy 2023-2028, confirms refugee financial inclusion remains a live gap being addressed through donor-funded projects rather than resolved access, consistent with "Partial."
